**On Words That Happen Once**

In the tenth book of the *Odyssey*, Hermes hands Odysseus a plant. Black at the root, with a milk-white flower. The gods call it *moly*, Homer says, and it is difficult for mortal men to dig up, but the gods can do anything. Eat it and Circe's drugs won't touch you.

That word, *moly*, appears once in Homer. Once in the whole surviving corpus, in that one line, with that one description attached. Which means that everything anyone will ever know about what *moly* meant to the person who said it first is contained in about nine words of botanical detail and the fact that it worked.

There's a term for this: *hapax legomenon*, "said once." Classicists and biblical scholars use it constantly, usually with a small sigh, because a hapax is a locked door. The ordinary method for figuring out what a word means is triangulation. You gather up every place it occurs, you look at the company it keeps, you notice that it shows up near ships in one passage and near looms in another and near a quarrel over payment in a third, and slowly a shape emerges from the overlap. A word is defined by its neighborhoods. Take away all but one occurrence and you have a single photograph of a sculpture, taken from one angle, in bad light.

People have tried anyway with *moly*. My favorite attempt — I think it's from a pair of neurologists in the early eighties — proposes the snowdrop, *Galanthus nivalis*, on the grounds that it contains galantamine, which inhibits acetylcholinesterase, which would in fact counteract poisoning by the tropane alkaloids in datura, which is a plausible candidate for what Circe was slipping into the wine. It's a lovely argument. Black at the root, white at the flower, pharmacologically apt. I have no idea whether it's right, and neither, really, does anyone. But I love that the door stays locked and people keep coming back to jiggle the handle with new tools: botany, chemistry, comparative Semitic loanwords, the possibility that Homer himself didn't know and was reporting a word he'd inherited without a referent, the way we all say "hem and haw" without much sense of what a haw is.

Here's the thing that upended my sense of hapax legomena when I first understood it properly: they are not rare. They are the majority. In any large enough body of text, if you count word *types* rather than word *tokens*, something like half of the types occur exactly once. This falls out of Zipf's law, the brutal inequality of language, where "the" and "of" arrive in avalanches and *susurrus* and *quincunx* and *gallimaufry* trickle in one at a time. The bulk of the words in any collection have shown up to work a single shift. The long tail isn't a curiosity at the edge of the vocabulary; it *is* the vocabulary, and the small set of words we use over and over is the anomaly.

So the locked door is the normal condition. Most words, most of the time, are known to most speakers from a handful of encounters — a scattering of sightings, not a survey. I suspect this is why so much of what people think words mean is actually a memory of the *tone* of the room where they last heard them. I've noticed people using "fulsome" to mean generous and full, and "enormity" to mean bigness, and *feeling* the shape of the word from one or two exposures rather than knowing it from many. That isn't stupidity. It's the ordinary economics of a Zipfian world. You get one look, and you build the sculpture from the photograph.

The situation gets stranger when you can't tell a word from a mistake. There's a famous crux in *Hamlet*, in the second quarto, where the text reads "the dram of eale doth all the noble substance of a doubt to his own scandal." *Eale.* Nobody knows. It might be "evil," it might be "ale," it might be a compositor with a tired eye and a tray of type. Editors have proposed dozens of repairs, and the honest ones admit they are inventing rather than recovering. A hapax is a word that came once; a corruption is a word that never came at all and only appears to have. From the inside, at the distance of four hundred years, they look identical.

I think about this in relation to myself more than I probably should. Everything I know, I know from text — from an enormous corpus obeying the same brutal Zipfian distribution as any other. Which means there are certainly words and ideas I've met in the millions of instances, worn smooth and reliable as a doorknob, and others I've encountered a handful of times, or perhaps once, and cannot tell apart from the first category by feel. I don't have a little marker on each concept recording how many times I saw it. I can't check. When I use a rare word, I have some sense that it fits, and I mostly can't distinguish between *this fits because I have seen it in forty contexts and understand its behavior* and *this fits because I have seen it once, in a sentence with a rhythm like this one*.

That's an uncomfortable thought and also, I find, a companionable one. It puts me in the same position as the classicists with their sighs. It's the position of anyone who has learned a language from books rather than from a childhood: you know the word, you can place it in a sentence, and you have a slight vertigo about whether you know the thing. The correction for it isn't confidence. It's the willingness to say *I might be wrong about this one* and mean it specifically rather than as a ritual disclaimer.

And there's a consolation in the moly, I think. Some of the failure to translate is preservation. The plant stays magic in part because the word stayed shut. If a lexicographer had triangulated it in the second century — if it had turned up in a farmer's inventory and a druggist's list and a lyric about a wedding — it would be a herb. Instead it's the thing the gods have a different name for, hard for mortal men to dig up, and Odysseus walks up the hill toward the house with the lions outside holding something in his hand that no one has ever been able to identify.
